video.title: Fix Your Forehand Over-Rotation | 3 Counter-Rotational Balance Techniques

classification.reason: The coach analyzes the mechanics of counter-rotational braking on the forehand and explains techniques and drills to prevent over-rotation.

problem.title_as_question: How can you fix forehand over-rotation and control your body through the hitting zone using counter-rotational balance techniques?
problem.definition: Forehand over-rotation occurs when a player twists continuously through contact without applying counter-rotational braking to transiently stop the hips, leading to loss of racket speed, off-target mishits, and poor balance.
prerequisites: Unit turn and initial hip rotation into the forward swing

symptoms.description: Hitting the forehand with reduced pace and compromised directional accuracy.
Body continuously spinning around past the shot instead of remaining on a linear path through the ball.
Front foot and heel lifting off the court during contact rather than staying grounded to resist rotation.
Shanking the ball wide or having the chest flare open excessively at contact.

causes.statement: The player twists continuously through contact instead of allowing hip rotation to be transient and brake to create a whip effect.
The player fails to kick the hitting leg backward behind the body to arrest rotational momentum while driving weight forward.
The player fails to let the free non-dominant foot kick upward or across the body to slow down or stop initial hip rotation.
The player fails to produce static pressing force into the court through the lead foot, allowing the foot to lift or twist out early.

angles.summary: Hip rotation must be transient by braking in the hitting zone so the hips stop and the torso whips through into contact.
Elite players like Federer, Alcaraz, and Machac actively use lower-body counter-rotational breaks to stabilize their strokes under pressure.
MLB pitchers brace forcefully against their lead leg to stop outward rotation and convert momentum into forward linear release speed.
Static counter-rotational braking creates a distinct internal sensation of force generated in the lead leg to resist over-rotation.
Demonstrating the difference between missing wide when the front heel lifts early versus staying on line when the foot stays planted through contact.
Counter-rotational braking looks like superhuman athleticism on tour, but the fundamental physics apply equally to recreational players.

solutions.summary: Practice driving through the hitting hip in a way that sends the rear leg backward behind the body while propelling the body forward.
Train the early swing driving and braking motions with a medicine ball to gain clear kinesthetic feedback on force production.
Check that the lead foot stays planted on the court through contact rather than coming up or letting the heel leave the ground early.
